name: Bambara kingdoms of Ségou and Kaarta
summary: Two Bambara kingdoms on the upper Niger: Kaarta (from about 1650) and Ségou (1712–1861), built on slave-soldier armies; the Toucouleur Empire conquered both.

location.value: The upper Niger valley, in today’s Mali.

climate.value: A Sahel climate with a short rainy season.

population.value: Ségou had around 30,000 inhabitants; the Bambara are about 40% of Mali’s population.

urbanisation.value: Mostly villages; a royal capital and market towns.

disease.value: Malaria and other tropical diseases; smallpox outbreaks.

migration.value: Captives taken in war were settled in farming villages.

economicBase.value: Farming worked by captive labour, and trade on the Niger.

tradeRoutes.value: Trade was carried by Muslim maraka merchants crossing the Sahara; Mamari conquered Djenné.

wealth.value: Tribute and war captives enriched the rulers.

moneyAndTax.value: Mamari introduced a tax system using cowrie shells as currency; cowries also raised tribute.

inequality.value: Slaves were divided into jonfin (saleable) and jonba (state labourers or soldiers); the army is described as one where class distinctions mattered little.

governmentType.value: A monarchy backed by a standing slave-soldier army.

keyRulers.value: Biton (Mamari) Coulibaly, first faama of the empire from 1712. Ngolo Diarra (seized the throne 1766; the article’s list gives 1766–1787).

succession.value: The Coulibaly dynasty first, followed by the Diarra dynasty in Ségou.

institutions.value: The ton, an age group that became a military aristocracy of tondjons.

stability.value: Rulers were deposed or assassinated by the ton djon, such as Dinkoro Coulibaly and Ali Coulibaly.

eliteConflict.value: Ségou and Kaarta fought each other, as well as neighbouring states.

armyAndTech.value: Infantry and war canoes on the Niger.

majorWars.value: Umar Tall declared jihad in 1859, took Nyamina in May 1860, and Ségou fell on 10 March 1861.

territoryChange.value: Expanded along the Niger in the 1700s.

alliancesRivals.value: The Fulani of Masina and, later, the Toucouleur were the main rivals.

scienceEducation.value: Oral learning; Qur’anic schools where Islam spread.

openness.value: Open to trade along the Niger, but hostile to rivals.

communicationTransport.value: Footpaths and the Niger River carried goods and news.

religion.value: Traditional religion: the faama was head priest of cults, and the kòmò resolved theological questions.

languageWriting.value: Bambara, a Mande language spoken by about 6 million people in Mali.

artsArchitecture.value: Chiwara headdresses, which honour the mythical antelope of farming.

sharedIdentity.value: Loyalty to the ruler, the lineage and Bambara traditions.

dailyLife.value: Families farmed millet and rice in villages, with warriors living in garrison towns.

ideasReligions.value: Bambara were defeated at Noukouma (1818) by Fula Muslim fighters of Cheikou Amadu’s jihad.

colonisation.value: Conquered by the Toucouleur, then France.

riseSignals.value: A Bambara kingdom existed in Ségou around 1640 (founder Kaladian Coulibaly); the centralised empire dates from 1712.

peakPeriod.value: Under Ngolo Diarra (seized the throne 1766); the article’s list gives 1766–1787, while its text says nearly thirty years.

outcome.value: Ségou fell to Umar Tall on 10 March 1861.

overallCertainty.value: Known from oral traditions, travellers and colonial records; many dates are approximate.
